articles.title: CRISPR-Engineered B Cells Dampen Autoimmune Responses in Mice
articles.text:
Skip to main content The Nutshell CRISPR-Engineered B Cells Dampen Autoimmune Responses in Mice Gene-edited regulatory B cells could suppress overactive immune responses, potentially helping in the treatment of autoimmune conditions like multiple sclerosis. Written by Rebecca Roberts, PhD Rebecca Roberts, PhD Rebecca Roberts is a science writer and communicator. She earned her PhD in molecular biology from the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia and completed a two-year postdoctoral fellowship at Lund University in Sweden. Her writing focuses on gene editing technology, cell and gene therapies, and the regulatory space. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 22, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later Gene-edited B cells could suppress disease-associated T cells and expand in response to autoimmune tissue damage. Image credit: © iStock.com, Rasi Bhadramani PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 3:00 Share B cells have enormous potential in the field of immunotherapy. By engineering B cells to express specific antibodies, researchers can use them as an alternative to vaccines for infectious diseases and circumvent issues associated with the production and storage of antibodies. 1 However, these cells could also be used to tamp down overactive immune responses seen in autoimmune conditions, such as multiple sclerosis (MS), lupus, and rheumatoid arthritis. Ragan Pitner , an immunologist at the University of Washington and the Seattle Children’s Research Institute is investigating this approach. During the “Engineered B-Cells as Therapeutic Agents” session of the 2026 annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy, Pitner discussed the application of engineered B cells to modulate immune responses in a mouse model of MS. “Multiple sclerosis is a neat model for this because B cells that accumulate within the meninges are known contributors to [the disease],” Pitner said. Decoy-Mediated Suppression with Engineered Bregs Regulatory B cells (Bregs) help orchestrate both innate and adaptive immune responses by secreting regulatory cytokines such as interleukin-10 and 35 and transforming growth factor beta. They also regulate the ability of other immune cells to present antigens and use their own antigen presentation machinery to modulate the activation and differentiation of helper T cells. Despite their potential, Bregs remain underutilized for therapeutic approaches. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Genomics updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe “The approaches that leverage natural Bregs as a cell therapy are unlikely to succeed,” Pitner explained. “Primarily because Bregs are highly heterogeneous.” This heterogeneity in Breg phenotype and function contributes to various autoimmune disorders. Unlike other immune cells, such as regulatory T cells, the Breg phenotype is also largely transient, Pitner said, meaning they don’t necessarily stay inhibitory when they are sorted and stimulated in the lab. Despite these challenges, Bregs are an attractive option for cell therapy because “In the people for whom Bregs would be the most useful, like people with autoimmune disease, [Bregs] are actually deficient,” Pitner added. To create Bregs that could modulate immune responses, Pitner and his colleagues, including his mentor, immunologist David Rawlings of the Seattle Children’s Hospital, developed a technique they call decoy-mediated suppression. The team genetically edited cultured B cells, preventing their maturation into antibody-secreting cells, then primed these gene-edited B cells with their antigens and transplanted them into mice immunized with the corresponding antigens. This resulted in the B cells expanding and dominating sites of B cell maturation, dulling the immune response to immunization. 3 “If you take this a step further, you ought to be able to put in a regulatory cargo to then take advantage of this antigen presentation, prevent the differentiation of more active inflammatory subsets like [pro-inflammatory T helper 1 and T helper 17 cells], and perhaps drive regulatory T cell differentiation,” said Pitner. Testing Engineered Bregs in a Mouse Model of Multiple Sclerosis Next, the team wanted to explore the effects of this approach in a mouse model of MS. They injected mice with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), a peptide that causes encephalitis and demyelination, which are hallmarks of MS. Pitner and his colleagues performed CRISPR editing in the B cells to prevent their maturation and insert regulatory cargo. The team found that these engineered Breg cells could successfully suppress disease-associated T cells, indicating potential in the treatment of autoimmune diseases. Finally, they investigated whether the edited Bregs could also respond to the production of antigens during autoimmune damage, such as myelin shedding. “These engineered antigen-specific B cells are preferentially expanded and retained in response to autoimmune tissue damage,” Pitner said about their currently unpublished data. The team is continuing to investigate the efficacy of the approach in models of MS. References Moffett HF, et al. B cells engineered to express pathogen-specific antibodies protect against infection . Sci Immunol. 2019;4(35):eaax0644. Pitner RA, et al. Blunting specific T-dependent antibody responses with engineered “decoy” B cells. Mol Ther. 2024;32(10):3453-3469. Trivedi N, et al. Engineering B cells to treat and study human disease . Apr 7, 2026 | 5 min read Save for Later A modern microvolume spectrophotometer enables rapid, low-volume quantification of nucleic acids and proteins, delivering critical concentration and purity data. Image credit: ©iStock, toondelamour PDF version Share Spectrophotometry remains a cornerstone of molecular biology, enabling rapid quantification and purity analysis of nucleic acids and proteins. In both research and teaching laboratories, advances in instrument design are improving accessibility without sacrificing accuracy. As a result, spectrophotometry continues to shape experimental reliability and reproducibility across the life sciences. Andy Jones Market Development Manager DeNovix In this Innovation Spotlight, Andy Jones , market development manager at DeNovix, discusses the challenges to accessing high-quality instrumentation and how emerging, cost-effective systems are addressing these barriers, expanding participation while maintaining rigorous data standards. What are the most common applications where spectrophotometry is indispensable in modern life science research laboratories? The most common applications for microvolume spectrophotometry are the quantification and quality control (QC) of nucleic acids and proteins. This is a fast, non-destructive method widely used in the life sciences that directly quantifies biomolecules based on their light absorbance at specific wavelengths using the Beer-Lambert law. For nucleic acids, quantification is one of the most routine tasks, with all nucleic acids having an absorbance peak at 260 nm. Sources may include genomic DNA, plasmids, or PCR products. Beyond simple quantification, the A260/A280 ratio is essential for assessing purity with regard to protein contamination, and the A260/A230 ratio indicates carryover of salts or solvents from extraction procedures. Both are crucial pieces of information before performing applications such as PCR, sequencing, or cloning. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cell Biology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe For protein quantification, proteins absorb UV light at a peak of 280 nm, largely because of the aromatic side chains of tryptophan and tyrosine. Because proteins are heterogeneous in this regard, the actual molar extinction coefficient can be calculated from the protein’s amino acid sequence. Total protein can also be quantified using colorimetric assays such as Bradford, BCA, and Lowry. Additionally, absorbance is used to quantify colorimetric signals in ELISA assays, making it essential in immunology and cell-based studies. Finally, cell growth monitoring relies on measuring optical density at 600 nm to track bacterial or yeast culture growth in real time. This is critical for determining when to induce protein expression, harvest cells, or conduct microbial experiments. In teaching laboratories, what role does hands-on access to spectrophotometers play in helping students understand core molecular biology concepts? Hands-on experience helps anchor abstract concepts from lectures to an observable, quantitative reality. It connects the idea that nucleic acids have aromatic rings that absorb UV light to real-world observations, linking "invisible" molecules such as nucleic acids and proteins to an absorbance value and concentration. Students also gain a practical understanding of the Beer-Lambert law. By plotting a dilution series, they learn about the linear range of the method, the limitations of the equipment, and the relationship between concentration, absorbance, and light pathlength. Crucially, they learn to understand quality as well as quantity. A student faced with purity ratios outside threshold values is forced to reason through the methodology of their experiment to determine where contamination—such as protein contamination, phenol carryover, or incorrect blanking—may have occurred, reinforcing the understanding that quantity without quality can cause issues with downstream applications. This technique, when linked to realistic downstream applications, allows the student to learn the cascading effect of sample quantity and quality through the entire analytical process, making the habit of revisiting quantification data of failed samples a critical research skill. Finally, it helps them understand that instruments are not "black-box answer machines." They learn to consider the steps involved in the analysis, what is happening on a chemical or biological level, the limitations of the methodology, and whether alternative methods are needed to supplement or corroborate findings. In teaching laboratories, hands-on use of spectrophotometers helps students connect molecular biology concepts to real data. ©iStock, Jacob Wackerhausen Why is access to reliable, research-grade instrumentation a challenge for many research and teaching laboratories today, particularly when it comes to spectrophotometry? And what obstacles do life science researchers and educators commonly face when assessing sample QC with outdated instruments? Research-grade instruments with high accuracy often require a significant investment, often in the thousands of US dollars. In teaching environments, accommodating numerous students can mean that the number of instruments is as important as their quality. This difficulty affects various settings. Undergraduate institutions often have limited grant infrastructure, labs in middle and lower-income countries may have dramatically smaller budgets, and new principal investigators often face limited startup funds when setting up a full lab. Continue reading below... Read More These practical constraints create a prohibitive barrier to accessing high-quality instrumentation. Laboratories often compromise by choosing low-cost methods such as gel quantification, sharing equipment with other labs, or relying on old or outdated instrumentation. The consequences in education are significant: students may not be trained on the equipment they will experience in a research environment, and the methods they learn might not be those currently employed. Running experiments on outdated or inaccurate equipment often leaves the student unable to differentiate between an instrument error and the precision of their own technique. Access to modern scientific equipment can attract high-quality students, and experience in current methods benefits both the student and future employers. On a broader level, poor quality data, often a result of outdated equipment, can lead to experimental inputs being poorly understood, a lack of traceability, difficulty replicating measurements within and between labs, and issues with publishing results or gaining regulatory approval for certified labs. How do modern spectrophotometers help overcome the above hurdles, and what design features make them approachable for new users without compromising data quality? Modern spectrophotometers for molecular biology applications address these challenges by employing microvolume pedestals rather than traditional cuvettes, which typically require 500 µL to 3 mL of sample. This enables easy biomolecule quantification in a few seconds with as little as 1 µL of sample. Traditionally, such instruments have been high-end investments. However, for research and teaching labs operating under tight budgets, the DeNovix Helium 1 µL Spectrophotometer offers a convergence of research-grade performance and genuine affordability, resolving the conflict of straining capital budgets versus using aging equipment that compromises data quality. The Helium is built on DeNovix SmartPath™ technology, the core technology of the DS-11 Series instruments used worldwide. For budget-conscious labs, the maintenance-free profile is particularly significant. It eliminates the hidden ongoing costs of lamp replacement, professional recalibration, and service contracts, ensuring data remains consistent and reliable over the lifetime of the instrument. The instrument quantifies double-stranded DNA between 2 and 1,600 ng/µL and protein between 0.1 and 48 mg/mL. Critical to QC, it provides built-in A260/A230 and A260/A280 purity ratios reported automatically. This covers the full range of routine sample QC without requiring additional software or manual calculation. For teaching laboratories, having purity ratios integrated as a default output reinforces good QC habits from the outset. For approachability, the stand-alone device includes a 7-inch HD touchscreen with simple, easy-to-use software. This eliminates the need for an external computer or IT setup, minimizing training overhead—all meaningful considerations when instrument time is shared across large student cohorts or research teams. How can accessible tools help democratize research, particularly for smaller laboratories, teaching-focused institutions, or resource-limited settings? Accessible and affordable instrumentation is fundamental to equitable science. When research-grade tools are available only to well-funded institutions, scientific participation is determined by resource access rather than intellectual merit. This narrows the talent pipeline and concentrates knowledge production in a small number of privileged settings. Instruments designed with genuine accessibility in mind—featuring low cost of ownership, intuitive operation, and maintenance-free reliability—change this dynamic. When the quality gap closes, a small teaching lab or a researcher in a resource-limited setting can produce data that meets the same quality standards as a flagship institution. This ultimately improves reproducibility, allows more voices to enter the literature, and makes science more truly global. Image credit: ©iStock, toondelamour PDF version Share Spectrophotometry remains a cornerstone of molecular biology, enabling rapid quantification and purity analysis of nucleic acids and proteins. In both research and teaching laboratories, advances in instrument design are improving accessibility without sacrificing accuracy. As a result, spectrophotometry continues to shape experimental reliability and reproducibility across the life sciences. Andy Jones Market Development Manager DeNovix In this Innovation Spotlight, Andy Jones , market development manager at DeNovix, discusses the challenges to accessing high-quality instrumentation and how emerging, cost-effective systems are addressing these barriers, expanding participation while maintaining rigorous data standards. What are the most common applications where spectrophotometry is indispensable in modern life science research laboratories? The most common applications for microvolume spectrophotometry are the quantification and quality control (QC) of nucleic acids and proteins. This is a fast, non-destructive method widely used in the life sciences that directly quantifies biomolecules based on their light absorbance at specific wavelengths using the Beer-Lambert law. For nucleic acids, quantification is one of the most routine tasks, with all nucleic acids having an absorbance peak at 260 nm. Sources may include genomic DNA, plasmids, or PCR products. Beyond simple quantification, the A260/A280 ratio is essential for assessing purity with regard to protein contamination, and the A260/A230 ratio indicates carryover of salts or solvents from extraction procedures. Both are crucial pieces of information before performing applications such as PCR, sequencing, or cloning. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cell Biology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe For protein quantification, proteins absorb UV light at a peak of 280 nm, largely because of the aromatic side chains of tryptophan and tyrosine. Because proteins are heterogeneous in this regard, the actual molar extinction coefficient can be calculated from the protein’s amino acid sequence. Total protein can also be quantified using colorimetric assays such as Bradford, BCA, and Lowry. Additionally, absorbance is used to quantify colorimetric signals in ELISA assays, making it essential in immunology and cell-based studies. Finally, cell growth monitoring relies on measuring optical density at 600 nm to track bacterial or yeast culture growth in real time. This is critical for determining when to induce protein expression, harvest cells, or conduct microbial experiments. In teaching laboratories, what role does hands-on access to spectrophotometers play in helping students understand core molecular biology concepts? Hands-on experience helps anchor abstract concepts from lectures to an observable, quantitative reality. It connects the idea that nucleic acids have aromatic rings that absorb UV light to real-world observations, linking "invisible" molecules such as nucleic acids and proteins to an absorbance value and concentration. Students also gain a practical understanding of the Beer-Lambert law. By plotting a dilution series, they learn about the linear range of the method, the limitations of the equipment, and the relationship between concentration, absorbance, and light pathlength. Crucially, they learn to understand quality as well as quantity. A student faced with purity ratios outside threshold values is forced to reason through the methodology of their experiment to determine where contamination—such as protein contamination, phenol carryover, or incorrect blanking—may have occurred, reinforcing the understanding that quantity without quality can cause issues with downstream applications. This technique, when linked to realistic downstream applications, allows the student to learn the cascading effect of sample quantity and quality through the entire analytical process, making the habit of revisiting quantification data of failed samples a critical research skill. Finally, it helps them understand that instruments are not "black-box answer machines." They learn to consider the steps involved in the analysis, what is happening on a chemical or biological level, the limitations of the methodology, and whether alternative methods are needed to supplement or corroborate findings. In teaching laboratories, hands-on use of spectrophotometers helps students connect molecular biology concepts to real data. ©iStock, Jacob Wackerhausen Why is access to reliable, research-grade instrumentation a challenge for many research and teaching laboratories today, particularly when it comes to spectrophotometry? And what obstacles do life science researchers and educators commonly face when assessing sample QC with outdated instruments? Research-grade instruments with high accuracy often require a significant investment, often in the thousands of US dollars. In teaching environments, accommodating numerous students can mean that the number of instruments is as important as their quality. This difficulty affects various settings. Undergraduate institutions often have limited grant infrastructure, labs in middle and lower-income countries may have dramatically smaller budgets, and new principal investigators often face limited startup funds when setting up a full lab. Read More These practical constraints create a prohibitive barrier to accessing high-quality instrumentation. Laboratories often compromise by choosing low-cost methods such as gel quantification, sharing equipment with other labs, or relying on old or outdated instrumentation. The consequences in education are significant: students may not be trained on the equipment they will experience in a research environment, and the methods they learn might not be those currently employed. Running experiments on outdated or inaccurate equipment often leaves the student unable to differentiate between an instrument error and the precision of their own technique. What are the most common applications where spectrophotometry is indispensable in modern life science research laboratories? The most common applications for microvolume spectrophotometry are the quantification and quality control (QC) of nucleic acids and proteins. This is a fast, non-destructive method widely used in the life sciences that directly quantifies biomolecules based on their light absorbance at specific wavelengths using the Beer-Lambert law. For nucleic acids, quantification is one of the most routine tasks, with all nucleic acids having an absorbance peak at 260 nm. Sources may include genomic DNA, plasmids, or PCR products. Beyond simple quantification, the A260/A280 ratio is essential for assessing purity with regard to protein contamination, and the A260/A230 ratio indicates carryover of salts or solvents from extraction procedures. Both are crucial pieces of information before performing applications such as PCR, sequencing, or cloning. Continue reading below... Like this story? Because proteins are heterogeneous in this regard, the actual molar extinction coefficient can be calculated from the protein’s amino acid sequence. Total protein can also be quantified using colorimetric assays such as Bradford, BCA, and Lowry. Additionally, absorbance is used to quantify colorimetric signals in ELISA assays, making it essential in immunology and cell-based studies. Finally, cell growth monitoring relies on measuring optical density at 600 nm to track bacterial or yeast culture growth in real time. This is critical for determining when to induce protein expression, harvest cells, or conduct microbial experiments. In teaching laboratories, what role does hands-on access to spectrophotometers play in helping students understand core molecular biology concepts? Hands-on experience helps anchor abstract concepts from lectures to an observable, quantitative reality. It connects the idea that nucleic acids have aromatic rings that absorb UV light to real-world observations, linking "invisible" molecules such as nucleic acids and proteins to an absorbance value and concentration. Students also gain a practical understanding of the Beer-Lambert law. By plotting a dilution series, they learn about the linear range of the method, the limitations of the equipment, and the relationship between concentration, absorbance, and light pathlength. Crucially, they learn to understand quality as well as quantity. A student faced with purity ratios outside threshold values is forced to reason through the methodology of their experiment to determine where contamination—such as protein contamination, phenol carryover, or incorrect blanking—may have occurred, reinforcing the understanding that quantity without quality can cause issues with downstream applications. This technique, when linked to realistic downstream applications, allows the student to learn the cascading effect of sample quantity and quality through the entire analytical process, making the habit of revisiting quantification data of failed samples a critical research skill. Finally, it helps them understand that instruments are not "black-box answer machines." They learn to consider the steps involved in the analysis, what is happening on a chemical or biological level, the limitations of the methodology, and whether alternative methods are needed to supplement or corroborate findings. articles.title: Fetal Gene Therapy Makes Strides Toward the Clinic
articles.text:
Skip to main content The Nutshell Fetal Gene Therapy Makes Strides Toward the Clinic A planned first-in-human trial aims to treat GM1 gangliosidosis in utero, possibly laying the foundation for prenatal gene therapies for other genetic diseases. Written by Rebecca Roberts, PhD Rebecca Roberts, PhD Rebecca Roberts is a science writer and communicator. She earned her PhD in molecular biology from the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia and completed a two-year postdoctoral fellowship at Lund University in Sweden. Her writing focuses on gene editing technology, cell and gene therapies, and the regulatory space. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 20, 2026 | 4 min read Save for Later After decades of success in preclinical large animal models, prenatal gene therapy is poised to begin first-in-human trials. GM1 gangliosidosis is one of the first targets. Image credit: © iStock.com, Nadiia Lapshynska PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 4:00 Share S cientists have had prenatal gene therapy in their sights for decades; by treating the fetus in utero, they can potentially prevent the long-term damage caused by severe, early-onset genetic disorders. Despite its success in preclinical studies , the method has not been successfully translated into human patients yet. However, that may soon change. Fetal surgeon Tippi MacKenzie hopes that once the therapy has been tested in GM1 gangliosidosis, they can broaden their scope to treat other genetic conditions in prenatal patients. Elisabeth Fall Last week, fetal surgeon Tippi MacKenzie of the University of California, San Francisco described the design of a phase I, first-in-human trial of a gene therapy for the treatment of GM1 gangliosidosis, a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder, in prenatal patients. “Evidence of safety and perhaps efficacy with this disease could allow us to unlock the field of clinical fetal gene therapy for related conditions,” MacKenzie remarked in her presentation during the ‘In Utero Therapeutics: Engineering Fetal Futures with Cell and Gene Therapy’ session at the 2026 annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy. Gaps in Clinical Translation of Fetal Gene Therapy Why has the clinical translation of fetal gene therapy been unsuccessful to date? According to MacKenzie, to move any fetal molecular therapy into clinical trials, it must meet stringent criteria: a robust genotype-to-phenotype correlation, strong evidence of anticipated benefit, established safety of the method when it is used postnatally, and a solid rationale for performing the treatment prenatally, rather than postnatally. Finally, work with patient advocacy groups must establish that the patient community wants the type of treatment in question. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Genetics updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe There are also more complicated safety considerations for prenatal therapies. “Fetal surgery is unique in that there are two patients, the mom and the fetus, and so both require close monitoring and long-term follow-up,” MacKenzie said. Fetal Gene Therapy for GM1 Gangliosidosis MacKenzie and her team have GM1 gangliosidosis in their sights as the first use case of fetal gene therapy. A severe, early-onset lysosomal storage disease, GM1 gangliosidosis is caused by mutations in the GLB1 gene encoding β-galactosidase—essential for breaking down complex sugars—resulting in the enzyme’s deficiency. This leads to progressive neurodegeneration and damage to the central nervous system, which cause spasticity, deafness, blindness, and seizures in patients; with no disease-modifying treatments available, the condition is fatal. 1 A previous phase I/II clinical trial by the National Human Genome Research Institute tested a gene therapy approach for GM1 gangliosidosis in postnatal patients, packaging the functional GLB1 gene in an adenoviral vector, AAV9. 2 “They determined that the AAV9- GLB1 [therapy] is safe and [leads to] some improvements in postnatal therapy, but it’s not transformative,” MacKenzie explained. “And so that's why we started [this project].” Because the treatment was considered safe but could not successfully produce durable responses in postnatal patients, MacKenzie and her team set their sights on prenatal patients. They designed a phase I, open-label, dose-escalating clinical trial to test the therapy in fetuses with the disease. “The primary objectives are safety and feasibility,” said MacKenzie. “Can we infuse this safely? Is it safe for [the] mom and [the] fetus? What are the immune responses to AAV9, and honestly, feasibility: Can we diagnose fetuses with GM1 early enough to be able to do this trial?” To monitor treatment efficacy, the team will test well-established biomarkers—including the β-galactosidase enzyme and GM1 ganglioside, a glycophospholipid expressed on the surface of neurons—in the amniotic fluid . However, these biomarkers are normally monitored in samples of cerebrospinal fluid, urine, and blood, MacKenzie said. “We're hoping to adapt these biomarker assays for amniotic fluid,” she added. Designing a Trial for Unborn Babies and Their Moms In designing the trial, MacKenzie and her team had to consider a range of other factors, including some unique to fetal therapies. For example, if the mother has pre-existing AAV9 antibodies, to what extent do they cross the placenta and impact efficacy? A 2024 study MacKenzie co-authored found the answers by injecting the umbilical vein of pregnant sheep with AAV9 carrying green fluorescent protein (GFP). 3 “When we infused fetal lambs with the AAV9-GFP vector, we do see anti-AAV9 antibodies in both the fetuses and the ewes,” MacKenzie commented. The PowerFlex™ Thermal Cycler delivers precise temperature gradient control, flexible workflows, and productivity features to help labs achieve reliable results and work more efficiently. Read More MacKenzie emphasized that despite advances in fetal monitoring, the fetus remains a “black box,” and there are many unknowns, including how to accurately measure fetal distress. “This is where we're poised to do a lot of research,” she said. “We're doing a lot of active research for biomarkers of fetal distress in maternal serum and amniotic fluids.” The team has submitted an investigational new drug (IND) application to the FDA for the therapy, which needs to be approved before they can begin enrolling their first patients. However, Mackenzie concluded that they hope to broaden the scope of the application in the near future. “The goal is to have this be part of a platform IND for other conditions that use similar vectors, because all of these conditions are individually very rare, and it’s even more rare to find an affected pregnancy,” she said. References Lang FM, et al. The natural history of type 1 infantile GM1 gangliosidosis: A literature-based meta-analysis . Mol Genet Metab . 2020;129(3):228-235. Lewis CJ, et al. AAV9 gene therapy in type II GM1 gangliosidosis - a phase 1-2 trial . N Engl J Med . 2026;394(12):1184-1194. Borges B, et al. Prenatal AAV9-GFP administration in fetal lambs results in transduction of female germ cells and maternal exposure to virus . Mol Ther Methods Clin Dev. 2024;32(2):101263. GM1 gangliosidosis is one of the first targets. Image credit: © iStock.com, Nadiia Lapshynska PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 4:00 Share S cientists have had prenatal gene therapy in their sights for decades; by treating the fetus in utero, they can potentially prevent the long-term damage caused by severe, early-onset genetic disorders. Despite its success in preclinical studies , the method has not been successfully translated into human patients yet. However, that may soon change. Fetal surgeon Tippi MacKenzie hopes that once the therapy has been tested in GM1 gangliosidosis, they can broaden their scope to treat other genetic conditions in prenatal patients. Elisabeth Fall Last week, fetal surgeon Tippi MacKenzie of the University of California, San Francisco described the design of a phase I, first-in-human trial of a gene therapy for the treatment of GM1 gangliosidosis, a rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorder, in prenatal patients. “Evidence of safety and perhaps efficacy with this disease could allow us to unlock the field of clinical fetal gene therapy for related conditions,” MacKenzie remarked in her presentation during the ‘In Utero Therapeutics: Engineering Fetal Futures with Cell and Gene Therapy’ session at the 2026 annual meeting of the American Society of Gene and Cell Therapy. Gaps in Clinical Translation of Fetal Gene Therapy Why has the clinical translation of fetal gene therapy been unsuccessful to date? According to MacKenzie, to move any fetal molecular therapy into clinical trials, it must meet stringent criteria: a robust genotype-to-phenotype correlation, strong evidence of anticipated benefit, established safety of the method when it is used postnatally, and a solid rationale for performing the treatment prenatally, rather than postnatally. Finally, work with patient advocacy groups must establish that the patient community wants the type of treatment in question. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Genetics updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe There are also more complicated safety considerations for prenatal therapies. “Fetal surgery is unique in that there are two patients, the mom and the fetus, and so both require close monitoring and long-term follow-up,” MacKenzie said. Fetal Gene Therapy for GM1 Gangliosidosis MacKenzie and her team have GM1 gangliosidosis in their sights as the first use case of fetal gene therapy. A severe, early-onset lysosomal storage disease, GM1 gangliosidosis is caused by mutations in the GLB1 gene encoding β-galactosidase—essential for breaking down complex sugars—resulting in the enzyme’s deficiency. This leads to progressive neurodegeneration and damage to the central nervous system, which cause spasticity, deafness, blindness, and seizures in patients; with no disease-modifying treatments available, the condition is fatal. 1 A previous phase I/II clinical trial by the National Human Genome Research Institute tested a gene therapy approach for GM1 gangliosidosis in postnatal patients, packaging the functional GLB1 gene in an adenoviral vector, AAV9. 2 “They determined that the AAV9- GLB1 [therapy] is safe and [leads to] some improvements in postnatal therapy, but it’s not transformative,” MacKenzie explained. “And so that's why we started [this project].” Because the treatment was considered safe but could not successfully produce durable responses in postnatal patients, MacKenzie and her team set their sights on prenatal patients. They designed a phase I, open-label, dose-escalating clinical trial to test the therapy in fetuses with the disease. “The primary objectives are safety and feasibility,” said MacKenzie. “Can we infuse this safely? Is it safe for [the] mom and [the] fetus? What are the immune responses to AAV9, and honestly, feasibility: Can we diagnose fetuses with GM1 early enough to be able to do this trial?” To monitor treatment efficacy, the team will test well-established biomarkers—including the β-galactosidase enzyme and GM1 ganglioside, a glycophospholipid expressed on the surface of neurons—in the amniotic fluid . However, these biomarkers are normally monitored in samples of cerebrospinal fluid, urine, and blood, MacKenzie said. “We're hoping to adapt these biomarker assays for amniotic fluid,” she added. Designing a Trial for Unborn Babies and Their Moms In designing the trial, MacKenzie and her team had to consider a range of other factors, including some unique to fetal therapies. For example, if the mother has pre-existing AAV9 antibodies, to what extent do they cross the placenta and impact efficacy? A 2024 study MacKenzie co-authored found the answers by injecting the umbilical vein of pregnant sheep with AAV9 carrying green fluorescent protein (GFP). 3 “When we infused fetal lambs with the AAV9-GFP vector, we do see anti-AAV9 antibodies in both the fetuses and the ewes,” MacKenzie commented. However, these biomarkers are normally monitored in samples of cerebrospinal fluid, urine, and blood, MacKenzie said. “We're hoping to adapt these biomarker assays for amniotic fluid,” she added.
amniotic fluid
Designing a Trial for Unborn Babies and Their Moms
In designing the trial, MacKenzie and her team had to consider a range of other factors, including some unique to fetal therapies. For example, if the mother has pre-existing AAV9 antibodies, to what extent do they cross the placenta and impact efficacy?
A 2024 study MacKenzie co-authored found the answers by injecting the umbilical vein of pregnant sheep with AAV9 carrying green fluorescent protein (GFP). 3 “When we infused fetal lambs with the AAV9-GFP vector, we do see anti-AAV9 antibodies in both the fetuses and the ewes,” MacKenzie commented.

MacKenzie emphasized that despite advances in fetal monitoring, the fetus remains a “black box,” and there are many unknowns, including how to accurately measure fetal distress. “This is where we're poised to do a lot of research,” she said. “We're doing a lot of active research for biomarkers of fetal distress in maternal serum and amniotic fluids.”
The team has submitted an investigational new drug (IND) application to the FDA for the therapy, which needs to be approved before they can begin enrolling their first patients. However, Mackenzie concluded that they hope to broaden the scope of the application in the near future. “The goal is to have this be part of a platform IND for other conditions that use similar vectors, because all of these conditions are individually very rare, and it’s even more rare to find an affected pregnancy,” she said.

articles.title: Human Organoids Expose Limits of Pancreatic Cancer Mouse Models
articles.text:
Skip to main content The Nutshell Human Organoids Expose Limits of Pancreatic Cancer Mouse Models A new stem-cell-derived model suggests human pancreatic cells require multiple genetic failures before becoming cancerous and lose key identity programs as tumors emerge. Written by Anirban Mukhopadhyay, PhD Anirban Mukhopadhyay, PhD Anirban Mukhopadhyay is an independent science journalist based in India with a PhD in genetics from Delhi University. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 19, 2026 | 3 min read Save for Later Researchers used human stem-cell-derived organoids to unlock the subtle genetic and epigenetic changes driving early pancreatic tumor formation. Image credit: © iStock.com, Mohammed Haneefa Nizamudeen PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 3:00 Share S cientists still do not fully understand how human pancreatic cells first become cancerous, limiting efforts to identify the disease at its earliest stages. “Early detection of pancreatic cancer is mostly missed because in 80 percent of cases, the tumor becomes symptomatic only after it has progressed to advanced stages,” said Jaskaran Singh Sethi , a radiation oncologist at Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Center, who was not involved in the study. Together, these challenges have made it difficult to identify early biomarkers or directly study the molecular events that initiate malignant transformation. 1 In a new study published in Developmental Cell , researchers developed human pancreatic organoids that reproduced the earliest stages of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) development and found that, unlike in many mouse models, activating the cancer-driving gene Kirsten rat sarcoma virus oncogene homologue ( KRAS ) alone was insufficient to drive tumor formation. 2 Instead, the human cells remained resistant unless multiple tumor-suppressive barriers were disrupted, suggesting that early pancreatic tumorigenesis in humans may be more complex than existing animal models have captured. The system also modeled progression toward aggressive forms of PDAC, potentially providing a platform to study early biomarkers and mechanisms of disease progression. For decades, genetically engineered mouse models have served as the dominant experimental system for studying pancreatic cancer initiation, helping establish oncogenic KRAS as a central driver of PDAC development. 3 However, increasing evidence suggested that malignant transformation in human pancreatic cells may require overcoming multiple tumor-suppressive barriers not fully captured in many mouse models. 4 Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe The question naturally arose: Which cellular states should scientists study to capture the early footprints of PDAC in humans? Previous work suggested that pancreatic injury and inflammation can trigger acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM), a regenerative reprogramming process in which mature pancreatic cells adopt a more plastic, progenitor-like state that may become permissive for tumor initiation. 5 To model this vulnerable state in a human system, researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Weill Cornell Medicine developed pancreatic organoids from human pluripotent stem cells. The organoids retained embryonic pancreatic progenitor features while also recapitulating molecular characteristics associated with inflamed pancreatic epithelium and ADM. Using this system, the researchers systematically introduced combinations of mutations commonly found in PDAC to test which genetic alterations were required for transformation. The researchers found that combining KRAS activation with loss of either the tumor suppressor genes cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A ( CDKN2A ) or tumor protein p53 ( TP53 ) still failed to produce tumors after transplantation into mice. However, organoids carrying KRAS activation together with loss of both CDKN2A and TP53 consistently formed pancreatic precursor lesions and moderately differentiated PDAC after transplantation. In particular, CDKN2A loss appeared necessary for KRAS - and TP53 -driven transformation, indicating that human pancreatic cells may possess stronger safeguards against malignant progression than traditional mouse systems have fully captured. An additional loss of SMAD family member 4 ( SMAD4 ) also drove progression toward a more aggressive, poorly differentiated, basal-like disease state associated with poorer clinical outcomes, suggesting that the organoid system can capture not only early tumor initiation, but also the emergence of clinically aggressive pancreatic cancer. 6 The researchers then examined how the organoids changed during malignant progression to better characterize the early molecular landscape of pancreatic tumorigenesis. They found that this transition involved two parallel shifts: activator protein 1 (AP-1) transcription factors appeared to drive the oncogenic side of this transition, promoting activation of malignant PDAC programs. At the same time, declining expression of ten-eleven translocation methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 ( TET1 ) weakened molecular programs linked to pancreatic lineage identity. The researchers traced both processes to ERK signaling activated by mutant KRAS , suggesting that the same pathway may simultaneously promote cancer-driving programs while dismantling mechanisms that preserve normal cellular identity. Together, the findings suggest that early pancreatic tumorigenesis may involve not only accumulation of oncogenic mutations, but also progressive erosion of the molecular features that maintain normal pancreatic identity. By modeling the earliest stages of human pancreatic cancer development, Sethi said, this “important study identifies key molecular and epigenetic events driving [malignant] transformation.” Such work has the potential to aid early detection, risk prediction, and development of preventive or targeted therapies, he said. Dec 31, 2025 | 3 min read Save for Later This postdoc studies how metabolic stress is sensed and relayed across organs to regulate growth and developmental timing. Image credit: Angelique di Domenico, ©iStock.com, aleksandarvelasevic PDF version Share Q | Write a brief introduction to yourself including the lab you work in and your research background. My name is Madhulika Rai . I am a developmental metabolism scientist with a strong interest in science communication, and I am also a passionate dancer. I moved to the United States to pursue postdoctoral research in Jason Tennessen’s laboratory at Indiana University Bloomington, where I investigated how metabolic processes influence organismal health and disease. Using Drosophila melanogaster as a model organism, my work focused on how metabolic stress in one tissue communicates with distant organs to regulate growth and developmental timing. I have recently joined Tania Reis’s laboratory at the University of Colorado-Anschutz, where I am excited to further expand my research toward understanding how brain function is coupled to systemic energy demands. Q | How did you first get interested in science and/or your field of research? My passion for science was sparked in high school, thanks to a biology teacher who encouraged me to explore the natural world beyond textbooks. That early inspiration led me to study biology in college, where I discovered research as a career option and quickly realized it was something I loved. Two professors played a key role in shaping my path: one introduced me to developmental biology and fruit flies ( Drosophila ), while the other sparked my interest in cancer biology. As a result of that, my PhD research was focused on finding suppressors of tumors in the brain using fruit flies. One of my findings while looking for suppressors, pivoted my brain in the field of metabolism. As I explored more, I realized that developmental metabolism is where I want to go next for postdoctoral research. Hence, that is what I do now. I use fruit flies and ask what if a key metabolic gene is absent: How do flies adapt to that stress and what can we learn from these adaptive mechanisms? Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cell Biology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Q | Tell us about your favorite research project you’re working on. Growing bodies need to carefully balance how much energy they take in and how much they use. In fruit flies, which grow rapidly as larvae, the brain plays a key role in sensing food and adjusting growth accordingly. I am currently invested in understanding how a brain protein called Activity-regulated cytoskeleton associated protein 1 (Arc1) – can regulate the bridge between what the animal eats and how fast it grows, helping maintain balance between energy and development. Q | What has been the most exciting part of your scientific career/journey so far? I would like to mention two parts that keep the excitement in my scientific journey- What excites me most about science is its universal language, shared across cultures and borders to explore, discover, and communicate. It has the power to transform how we understand nature. There's something deeply inspiring in knowing that while I may not live forever, the knowledge I uncover can endure and might benefit society for generations to come. Another part of my journey that excites me is mentorship because it allows me to nurture curiosity, build confidence, and support growth in young minds. I love helping students discover their potential, whether it's guiding them through complex scientific questions or encouraging resilience when experiments don’t go as planned. Each student brings a unique perspective, and I learn as much from them as they do from me. Creating a supportive environment where students feel empowered to ask questions and explore ideas is deeply rewarding and exciting. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a microscope because it reveals hidden worlds, opening our eyes to the fascinating universe of microorganisms that exist beyond what we can see. Growing bodies need to carefully balance how much energy they take in and how much they use. In fruit flies, which grow rapidly as larvae, the brain plays a key role in sensing food and adjusting growth accordingly. I am currently invested in understanding how a brain protein called Activity-regulated cytoskeleton associated protein 1 (Arc1) – can regulate the bridge between what the animal eats and how fast it grows, helping maintain balance between energy and development. Q | What has been the most exciting part of your scientific career/journey so far? I would like to mention two parts that keep the excitement in my scientific journey- What excites me most about science is its universal language, shared across cultures and borders to explore, discover, and communicate. It has the power to transform how we understand nature. There's something deeply inspiring in knowing that while I may not live forever, the knowledge I uncover can endure and might benefit society for generations to come. Another part of my journey that excites me is mentorship because it allows me to nurture curiosity, build confidence, and support growth in young minds. I love helping students discover their potential, whether it's guiding them through complex scientific questions or encouraging resilience when experiments don’t go as planned. Each student brings a unique perspective, and I learn as much from them as they do from me. Creating a supportive environment where students feel empowered to ask questions and explore ideas is deeply rewarding and exciting. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a microscope because it reveals hidden worlds, opening our eyes to the fascinating universe of microorganisms that exist beyond what we can see. The system also modeled progression toward aggressive forms of PDAC, potentially providing a platform to study early biomarkers and mechanisms of disease progression. For decades, genetically engineered mouse models have served as the dominant experimental system for studying pancreatic cancer initiation, helping establish oncogenic KRAS as a central driver of PDAC development. 3 However, increasing evidence suggested that malignant transformation in human pancreatic cells may require overcoming multiple tumor-suppressive barriers not fully captured in many mouse models. 4 Continue reading below... Previous work suggested that pancreatic injury and inflammation can trigger acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM), a regenerative reprogramming process in which mature pancreatic cells adopt a more plastic, progenitor-like state that may become permissive for tumor initiation. 5 To model this vulnerable state in a human system, researchers at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Weill Cornell Medicine developed pancreatic organoids from human pluripotent stem cells. The organoids retained embryonic pancreatic progenitor features while also recapitulating molecular characteristics associated with inflamed pancreatic epithelium and ADM. Using this system, the researchers systematically introduced combinations of mutations commonly found in PDAC to test which genetic alterations were required for transformation. The researchers found that combining KRAS activation with loss of either the tumor suppressor genes cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A ( CDKN2A ) or tumor protein p53 ( TP53 ) still failed to produce tumors after transplantation into mice. However, organoids carrying KRAS activation together with loss of both CDKN2A and TP53 consistently formed pancreatic precursor lesions and moderately differentiated PDAC after transplantation. In particular, CDKN2A loss appeared necessary for KRAS - and TP53 -driven transformation, indicating that human pancreatic cells may possess stronger safeguards against malignant progression than traditional mouse systems have fully captured. An additional loss of SMAD family member 4 ( SMAD4 ) also drove progression toward a more aggressive, poorly differentiated, basal-like disease state associated with poorer clinical outcomes, suggesting that the organoid system can capture not only early tumor initiation, but also the emergence of clinically aggressive pancreatic cancer. 6 The researchers then examined how the organoids changed during malignant progression to better characterize the early molecular landscape of pancreatic tumorigenesis. They found that this transition involved two parallel shifts: activator protein 1 (AP-1) transcription factors appeared to drive the oncogenic side of this transition, promoting activation of malignant PDAC programs. At the same time, declining expression of ten-eleven translocation methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 ( TET1 ) weakened molecular programs linked to pancreatic lineage identity. The researchers traced both processes to ERK signaling activated by mutant KRAS , suggesting that the same pathway may simultaneously promote cancer-driving programs while dismantling mechanisms that preserve normal cellular identity. Together, the findings suggest that early pancreatic tumorigenesis may involve not only accumulation of oncogenic mutations, but also progressive erosion of the molecular features that maintain normal pancreatic identity. By modeling the earliest stages of human pancreatic cancer development, Sethi said, this “important study identifies key molecular and epigenetic events driving [malignant] transformation.” Such work has the potential to aid early detection, risk prediction, and development of preventive or targeted therapies, he said. Image credit: Angelique di Domenico, ©iStock.com, aleksandarvelasevic PDF version Share Q | Write a brief introduction to yourself including the lab you work in and your research background. My name is Madhulika Rai . I am a developmental metabolism scientist with a strong interest in science communication, and I am also a passionate dancer. I moved to the United States to pursue postdoctoral research in Jason Tennessen’s laboratory at Indiana University Bloomington, where I investigated how metabolic processes influence organismal health and disease. Using Drosophila melanogaster as a model organism, my work focused on how metabolic stress in one tissue communicates with distant organs to regulate growth and developmental timing. I have recently joined Tania Reis’s laboratory at the University of Colorado-Anschutz, where I am excited to further expand my research toward understanding how brain function is coupled to systemic energy demands. Q | How did you first get interested in science and/or your field of research? My passion for science was sparked in high school, thanks to a biology teacher who encouraged me to explore the natural world beyond textbooks. That early inspiration led me to study biology in college, where I discovered research as a career option and quickly realized it was something I loved. Two professors played a key role in shaping my path: one introduced me to developmental biology and fruit flies ( Drosophila ), while the other sparked my interest in cancer biology. As a result of that, my PhD research was focused on finding suppressors of tumors in the brain using fruit flies. One of my findings while looking for suppressors, pivoted my brain in the field of metabolism. As I explored more, I realized that developmental metabolism is where I want to go next for postdoctoral research. Hence, that is what I do now. I use fruit flies and ask what if a key metabolic gene is absent: How do flies adapt to that stress and what can we learn from these adaptive mechanisms? Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cell Biology updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Q | Tell us about your favorite research project you’re working on. Growing bodies need to carefully balance how much energy they take in and how much they use. In fruit flies, which grow rapidly as larvae, the brain plays a key role in sensing food and adjusting growth accordingly. I am currently invested in understanding how a brain protein called Activity-regulated cytoskeleton associated protein 1 (Arc1) – can regulate the bridge between what the animal eats and how fast it grows, helping maintain balance between energy and development. Q | What has been the most exciting part of your scientific career/journey so far? I would like to mention two parts that keep the excitement in my scientific journey- What excites me most about science is its universal language, shared across cultures and borders to explore, discover, and communicate. It has the power to transform how we understand nature. There's something deeply inspiring in knowing that while I may not live forever, the knowledge I uncover can endure and might benefit society for generations to come. Another part of my journey that excites me is mentorship because it allows me to nurture curiosity, build confidence, and support growth in young minds. I love helping students discover their potential, whether it's guiding them through complex scientific questions or encouraging resilience when experiments don’t go as planned. Each student brings a unique perspective, and I learn as much from them as they do from me. Creating a supportive environment where students feel empowered to ask questions and explore ideas is deeply rewarding and exciting. Q | If you could be a laboratory instrument, which one would you be and why? I would be a microscope because it reveals hidden worlds, opening our eyes to the fascinating universe of microorganisms that exist beyond what we can see. articles.title: Cargo-free LNP Manufacturing Could Spark a Nucleic Acid Therapy Renaissance
articles.text:
Skip to main content Opinion Cargo-free LNP Manufacturing Could Spark a Nucleic Acid Therapy Renaissance Combining pre-formed vesicles with nucleic acid cargo at the point of care can remove long-standing barriers to personalized nucleic acid therapeutics. Written by Ying K. Tam, PhD Ying K. Tam, PhD Ying K. Tam, PhD, Chief Scientific Officer of Acuitas Therapeutics, is a globally recognised expert in nanotechnology and immunology with more than 100 peer-reviewed publications. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . and Paulo Lin, PhD Paulo Lin, PhD Paulo Lin, PhD, Sr. Director of Formulation Development at Acuitas Therapeutics, has nearly 20 years in lipid nanoparticles, supporting hundreds of programs and more than 30 licensed products worldwide. View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . May 16, 2026 | 6 min read Save for Later Waiting to combine pre-formed vesicles (PFVs) with their nucleic acid therapies at the point of care instead of manufacturing pre-loaded lipid nanoparticles could lead to faster turnaround times and enable smaller batch production. Image credit: © iStock.com, koto_feja PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 6:00 Share T he Elegance of Nucleic Acid Therapy is Compromised by Logistic Complexity Conventional biologics are static; their structure and mechanism are fixed once they are developed. In contrast, nucleic acid therapies are inherently programmable—putting treatments once thought to be impossible within reach. The attractiveness of using RNA or DNA as a therapeutic comes from the nature of a nucleic acid itself, which can encode a plethora of biological outcomes based on the type of nucleic acid and the nucleotide sequence. 1 To elicit a targeted immune response, mRNA encoding an antigen can function as a vaccine, while mRNA encoding antibodies can mimic an adaptive immune response. To intervene at the level of disease-causing molecular mechanisms, siRNA can silence disease-causing genes; mRNA can replace missing proteins; and targeted gene editing can be achieved when a guide RNA is paired with mRNA encoding a gene editor. 1 Small adjustments to a nucleic acid design enable further tailoring of a nucleic acid therapy’s mechanism of action, and can lead to improvements in stability, potency, and safety. This enables amendments at the drug substrate level without changing the overall drug product design. 1 For instance, modifying the coding sequence of an antigenic protein can allow an mRNA vaccine platform to be adapted to the biology of a specific recipient or pathogenic target, without changing the overarching approach or mechanism. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Newsletter updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe This programmability makes nucleic acid therapies uniquely well-suited to rapidly respond to quickly evolving infectious diseases and to the development of personalized medicines . Yet, current manufacturing and delivery models for nucleic acid therapies are based on processes that assume large-batch production of a fixed product, and this limits the inherent flexibility of nucleic acid therapeutics, thus reducing their therapeutic application. 2 An alternative process that combines cargo-agnostic pre-formed vesicles (PFVs) with the customizable therapeutic agent at the point-of-care could help nucleic acid therapies enable personalized medicines. 3 How Are Nucleic Acid Therapies Made Today? This type of therapy includes a highly fragile and biologically reactive nucleic acid cargo, which acts as the therapeutic agent, and a delivery vehicle, which encapsulates the cargo to protect it and facilitate entry into target cells. A commonly used and clinically validated delivery vehicle for nucleic acid therapies, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), are constructed from a precise mix of ionizable lipids, structural lipids, and steric lipids—each playing a critical role. These include interacting with, encapsulating, and protecting the nucleic acid payload. Together, the formulation of an LNP determines how well it maintains stability and purity during manufacturing and administration as well as the success of cellular delivery and uptake. 4 For special applications, LNPs can be decorated with ligands which enable cell-specific delivery. Current manufacturing and shipping processes for nucleic acid therapies involve loading the delivery vehicle with the nucleic acid cargo upfront. This requires relatively large batch sizes and complex procedures to maintain the integrity and stability of the product over time. 2 In this loading process, the lipid components of the LNPs are combined and dissolved in an organic solvent (typically ethanol), and rapidly mixed with the nucleic acid cargo suspended in an acidic buffer, assembling themselves into LNPs that completely encapsulate the nucleic acid therapeutic. The ethanol must then be removed and replaced with an isotonic neutral pH buffer to stabilize the loaded LNPs, before the products are prepared for cryopreservation, vialed, frozen, and shipped via cold-chain (typically -20°C to -80°C). 2 While working on the COMIRNATY™ vaccine process with Pfizer and BioNTech, we found that this manufacturing model is sensible when large batches of a nucleic acid therapy are needed to address a pandemic-scale response. 4 However, the resulting products required cold-chain infrastructure and needed to be received and administered by hospital personnel trained in handling cryopreserved products, limiting vaccine access in low-resource settings. The manufacturing model was also wasteful; as the COVID-19 virus mutated, the efficacy of the original vaccine design waned, necessitating a yearly update to the formulation. Re-manufacturing the vaccine with an updated mRNA sequence led to the waste of the previous year’s unused vaccines. In most contexts where a nucleic acid therapy’s modality is most promising, upfront batch-based production is counterproductive, necessitating over-production that increases the cost of a nucleic acid therapy on a per-dose basis. The excessive minimum-batch sizes of current production methods limit the economic feasibility of single, small-batch therapies and of therapeutic iteration. Meanwhile, pre-loading of the delivery vehicle with nucleic acid cargo ties therapeutic modification-to-administration turnaround times to the combined manufacturing, release, and shipping process which can take upwards of six months. 2 Processes that enable smaller-scale production and shorter turnaround times between therapeutic modification and administration are needed to propel rapidly programmable medicines from possibility to clinical reality. Pre-formed Vesicles Could Resolve LNP Manufacturing Bottlenecks Loading PFVs with their nucleic acid cargo at the point-of-care has the potential to resolve many of these manufacturing bottlenecks for highly personalized and time-sensitive nucleic acid therapies by enabling much smaller-scale production of nucleic acid cargo and shortening timelines for platform modification. By manufacturing PFVs separately from their cargo, large batches of PFVs can be manufactured ahead of time, in a process analogous to normal LNP production. PFVs can then be combined at the point-of-care with nucleic acid cargo, which can be developed on much shorter timelines and in appropriate quantities for small-scale administration. 3 Conventional and PFV-based methods of therapeutic delivery vary in the required batch size of the RNA-LNP product, the timing of final-product formulation, and their storage requirements. Acuitas Therapeutics Moreover, manufacturing and shipping PFVs separately from nucleic acid cargo allows for tailored preservation and storage techniques that are less dependent on cold-chain shipping and storage for the delivery vehicle (The nucleic acid cargo may still require cold-chain shipping and storage). Compared to pre-assembled therapies, PFVs can be stored at higher temperatures and shipped in a liquid format while maintaining stability. Preclinical Evidence Sets the Stage for Clinical Development Preclinical testing demonstrates that PFVs can be assembled with nucleic acid cargo within 10–20 minutes at the point-of-care without heat or solvents. With optimized buffer, researchers observed over 90 percent encapsulation efficiency across a variety of payloads, including mRNA, siRNA, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), and mRNA/gRNA mixes at a 1:1 ratio. Due to the reduced interaction time between LNP and mRNA, the PFV process has shown decreased formation of unwanted RNA-lipid adducts compared to conventional mixing methods. 3 Physical and chemical analysis of formulations produced by the conventional and PFV methods show that the particle properties are indistinguishable between both processes. These measurements included particle size and polydispersity index, encapsulation efficiency, RNA content, lipid content, and RNA integrity. Moreover, morphological analysis by cryo-EM imaging showed equivalent particles, and PFV loaded with mRNA demonstrated stability for over 40 weeks in liquid-format storage conditions (2–8 o C). 3 The most compelling stability readout showed unloaded PFV’s unique ability to retain encapsulation efficacy across all time points over a 12 month period when stored in non-frozen, liquid form (4 o C) or cryopreserved (-80 o C), while retaining colloidal stability (unchanging size and a polydispersity index under 0.1) across storage conditions. 3 The capacity for long-term storage suggests the delivery vehicle of a nucleic acid therapy can be stored in bulk at the point-of-care so that the timing of therapeutic administration is primarily contingent upon the availability of nucleic acid cargo. LNP-RNA products manufactured through the standard loading process (Std) and the PFV process demonstrate equivalent hemagglutinin (HA) antigen response across LNP ionizable lipid compositions. Acuitas Therapeutics In a proof-of-concept where the PFV was produced immediately before administration, researchers demonstrated equivalent performance between the two delivery methods across different applications: prophylactic vaccines and systemically administered therapeutics. For an mRNA vaccine encoding an influenza hemagglutinin (HA) antigen, functional antibody response was statistically equivalent between conventional LNP and PFV. For systemically administered therapeutics, comparable serum antibody expression was also achieved following delivery of mRNA encoding a monoclonal antibody. 3 While PFVs have yet to be applied in clinical trials, preclinical evidence to date supports the long-term potential to improve the feasibility of programmable medicine. Drug developers working on vaccine strategies for rapidly evolving pathogens and those working on highly personalized and programmable nucleic acid medicines may benefit from an investment in this novel manufacturing strategy. LNP-RNA products encoding the monoclonal antibody IgG that are manufactured through the standard loading process (Conventional mixing) and the point-of-care PFV process have comparable serum antibody expression response. Acuitas Therapeutics A Convergence of Nucleic Acid Therapeutic Innovation The PFV manufacturing method converges in time with many other advancements that are broadening the accessibility and applications of nucleic acid medicines. Improved understanding of nucleic acid and disease biology is expanding the forms and applications of nucleic acid cargo. 1,4 Change is incremental but hastened by the collaboration of teams who bring together diverse solutions and approaches to better address enduring threats to human health and well-being. Dec 23, 2025 | 2 min read Save for Later Combining pharmaceutical sciences and cancer biology, this postdoc studies next-generation drug delivery systems. Image credit: Coptis, ©iStock.com, Olemedia PDF version Share Q | Write a brief introduction to yourself including the lab you work in and your research background. I am Deepika Godugu , and I am currently a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences at St. John’s University. My research focuses on anticancer drug development and evaluation, with expertise in both in vitro cell-based assays and in vivo tumor models. I have a strong background in pharmaceutical sciences, cancer biology, and advanced drug delivery systems, including nanotechnology-based formulations. My technical skills include molecular biology techniques such as Western blotting, flow cytometry, PCR, and functional gene silencing approaches including shRNA transfection and lentiviral transduction. Q | How did you first get interested in science and/or your field of research? My interest in science began during my undergraduate studies in pharmacy, where I was fascinated by how molecular mechanisms could be targeted to treat disease. This curiosity deepened during my PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences, where I worked on developing and evaluating novel drug delivery systems for cancer therapy. Witnessing the limitations of conventional treatments, especially in oncology, motivated me to explore innovative approaches such as nanomedicine, targeted delivery, and molecular interventions. I was particularly drawn to translational research that bridges laboratory discoveries with clinical applications. My postdoctoral work at St. John’s University has allowed me to combine in vitro assays, in vivo tumor models, and molecular biology techniques such as shRNA-mediated gene silencing to better understand therapeutic mechanisms and resistance pathways. This integration of basic science with potential real-world impact continues to inspire my research, with the ultimate goal of improving patient outcomes through more precise and effective therapies. Continue reading below... Like this story? Sign up for FREE Cancer updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe Q | Tell us about your favorite research project you’re working on. One of my favorite research projects focuses on developing a nanoparticle-based formulation to enhance the delivery and efficacy of an anticancer compound with poor bioavailability. This project is exciting because it combines my expertise in pharmaceutical formulation with molecular biology approaches to evaluate therapeutic mechanisms. Using in vitro cancer cell models and in vivo tumor-bearing mice, we assess not only the drug’s cytotoxicity but also its ability to modulate specific molecular pathways linked to tumor growth and resistance. What I find most rewarding is the translational potential our preclinical results show promising tumor regression and reduced systemic toxicity, bringing the formulation a step closer to potential clinical application. The project also incorporates advanced techniques like shRNA-mediated gene silencing to dissect the drug’s mechanism of action, which adds a deeper mechanistic layer to our findings. Seeing the intersection of formulation science, molecular targeting, and therapeutic efficacy makes this work both challenging and inspiring. Q | What has been the most exciting part of your scientific career/journey so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey so far has been seeing a research concept evolve from an initial idea to promising preclinical results with real translational potential. During my PhD and postdoctoral work, I have had the opportunity to design novel drug formulations, test them in both cell-based and animal models, and uncover their molecular mechanisms of action. One highlight was developing a nanoparticle-based anticancer formulation that significantly improved therapeutic efficacy and reduced toxicity in vivo. Watching data emerge that could eventually inform better treatment strategies was both professionally fulfilling and personally motivating. Moments like these when rigorous experimentation leads to discoveries that could meaningfully impact patient care reinforce why I chose a career in translational cancer research. I am Deepika Godugu , and I am currently a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences at St. John’s University. My research focuses on anticancer drug development and evaluation, with expertise in both in vitro cell-based assays and in vivo tumor models. I have a strong background in pharmaceutical sciences, cancer biology, and advanced drug delivery systems, including nanotechnology-based formulations. My technical skills include molecular biology techniques such as Western blotting, flow cytometry, PCR, and functional gene silencing approaches including shRNA transfection and lentiviral transduction. Q | How did you first get interested in science and/or your field of research? My interest in science began during my undergraduate studies in pharmacy, where I was fascinated by how molecular mechanisms could be targeted to treat disease. This curiosity deepened during my PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences, where I worked on developing and evaluating novel drug delivery systems for cancer therapy. Witnessing the limitations of conventional treatments, especially in oncology, motivated me to explore innovative approaches such as nanomedicine, targeted delivery, and molecular interventions. I was particularly drawn to translational research that bridges laboratory discoveries with clinical applications. My postdoctoral work at St. John’s University has allowed me to combine in vitro assays, in vivo tumor models, and molecular biology techniques such as shRNA-mediated gene silencing to better understand therapeutic mechanisms and resistance pathways. This integration of basic science with potential real-world impact continues to inspire my research, with the ultimate goal of improving patient outcomes through more precise and effective therapies. One of my favorite research projects focuses on developing a nanoparticle-based formulation to enhance the delivery and efficacy of an anticancer compound with poor bioavailability. This project is exciting because it combines my expertise in pharmaceutical formulation with molecular biology approaches to evaluate therapeutic mechanisms. Using in vitro cancer cell models and in vivo tumor-bearing mice, we assess not only the drug’s cytotoxicity but also its ability to modulate specific molecular pathways linked to tumor growth and resistance. What I find most rewarding is the translational potential our preclinical results show promising tumor regression and reduced systemic toxicity, bringing the formulation a step closer to potential clinical application. The project also incorporates advanced techniques like shRNA-mediated gene silencing to dissect the drug’s mechanism of action, which adds a deeper mechanistic layer to our findings. Seeing the intersection of formulation science, molecular targeting, and therapeutic efficacy makes this work both challenging and inspiring. Q | What has been the most exciting part of your scientific career/journey so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey so far has been seeing a research concept evolve from an initial idea to promising preclinical results with real translational potential. During my PhD and postdoctoral work, I have had the opportunity to design novel drug formulations, test them in both cell-based and animal models, and uncover their molecular mechanisms of action. One highlight was developing a nanoparticle-based anticancer formulation that significantly improved therapeutic efficacy and reduced toxicity in vivo. Watching data emerge that could eventually inform better treatment strategies was both professionally fulfilling and personally motivating. Moments like these when rigorous experimentation leads to discoveries that could meaningfully impact patient care reinforce why I chose a career in translational cancer research. Written by Ying K. Tam, PhD Ying K. Tam, PhD Ying K.
