May 16, 2026 | 6 min read Save for Later Waiting to combine pre-formed vesicles (PFVs) with their nucleic acid therapies at the point of care instead of manufacturing pre-loaded lipid nanoparticles could lead to faster turnaround times and enable smaller batch production. Image credit: © iStock.com, koto_feja PDF version Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 6:00 Share T he Elegance of Nucleic Acid Therapy is Compromised by Logistic Complexity Conventional biologics are static; their structure and mechanism are fixed once they are developed. In contrast, nucleic acid therapies are inherently programmable—putting treatments once thought to be impossible within reach. The attractiveness of using RNA or DNA as a therapeutic comes from the nature of a nucleic acid itself, which can encode a plethora of biological outcomes based on the type of nucleic acid and the nucleotide sequence. 1 To elicit a targeted immune response, mRNA encoding an antigen can function as a vaccine, while mRNA encoding antibodies can mimic an adaptive immune response. To intervene at the level of disease-causing molecular mechanisms, siRNA can silence disease-causing genes; mRNA can replace missing proteins; and targeted gene editing can be achieved when a guide RNA is paired with mRNA encoding a gene editor. 1 Small adjustments to a nucleic acid design enable further tailoring of a nucleic acid therapy’s mechanism of action, and can lead to improvements in stability, potency, and safety. This enables amendments at the drug substrate level without changing the overall drug product design. 1 For instance, modifying the coding sequence of an antigenic protein can allow an mRNA vaccine platform to be adapted to the biology of a specific recipient or pathogenic target, without changing the overarching approach or mechanism. Sign up for FREE Newsletter updates: Latest science news stories Topic-tailored resources and events Customized newsletter content Subscribe This programmability makes nucleic acid therapies uniquely well-suited to rapidly respond to quickly evolving infectious diseases and to the development of personalized medicines . Yet, current manufacturing and delivery models for nucleic acid therapies are based on processes that assume large-batch production of a fixed product, and this limits the inherent flexibility of nucleic acid therapeutics, thus reducing their therapeutic application. 2 An alternative process that combines cargo-agnostic pre-formed vesicles (PFVs) with the customizable therapeutic agent at the point-of-care could help nucleic acid therapies enable personalized medicines. 3 How Are Nucleic Acid Therapies Made Today? This type of therapy includes a highly fragile and biologically reactive nucleic acid cargo, which acts as the therapeutic agent, and a delivery vehicle, which encapsulates the cargo to protect it and facilitate entry into target cells. A commonly used and clinically validated delivery vehicle for nucleic acid therapies, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), are constructed from a precise mix of ionizable lipids, structural lipids, and steric lipids—each playing a critical role. These include interacting with, encapsulating, and protecting the nucleic acid payload. Together, the formulation of an LNP determines how well it maintains stability and purity during manufacturing and administration as well as the success of cellular delivery and uptake. 4 For special applications, LNPs can be decorated with ligands which enable cell-specific delivery. Current manufacturing and shipping processes for nucleic acid therapies involve loading the delivery vehicle with the nucleic acid cargo upfront. This requires relatively large batch sizes and complex procedures to maintain the integrity and stability of the product over time. 2 In this loading process, the lipid components of the LNPs are combined and dissolved in an organic solvent (typically ethanol), and rapidly mixed with the nucleic acid cargo suspended in an acidic buffer, assembling themselves into LNPs that completely encapsulate the nucleic acid therapeutic. The ethanol must then be removed and replaced with an isotonic neutral pH buffer to stabilize the loaded LNPs, before the products are prepared for cryopreservation, vialed, frozen, and shipped via cold-chain (typically -20°C to -80°C). 2 While working on the COMIRNATY™ vaccine process with Pfizer and BioNTech, we found that this manufacturing model is sensible when large batches of a nucleic acid therapy are needed to address a pandemic-scale response. 4 However, the resulting products required cold-chain infrastructure and needed to be received and administered by hospital personnel trained in handling cryopreserved products, limiting vaccine access in low-resource settings. The manufacturing model was also wasteful; as the COVID-19 virus mutated, the efficacy of the original vaccine design waned, necessitating a yearly update to the formulation. Re-manufacturing the vaccine with an updated mRNA sequence led to the waste of the previous year’s unused vaccines. In most contexts where a nucleic acid therapy’s modality is most promising, upfront batch-based production is counterproductive, necessitating over-production that increases the cost of a nucleic acid therapy on a per-dose basis. The excessive minimum-batch sizes of current production methods limit the economic feasibility of single, small-batch therapies and of therapeutic iteration. Meanwhile, pre-loading of the delivery vehicle with nucleic acid cargo ties therapeutic modification-to-administration turnaround times to the combined manufacturing, release, and shipping process which can take upwards of six months. 2 Processes that enable smaller-scale production and shorter turnaround times between therapeutic modification and administration are needed to propel rapidly programmable medicines from possibility to clinical reality. Pre-formed Vesicles Could Resolve LNP Manufacturing Bottlenecks Loading PFVs with their nucleic acid cargo at the point-of-care has the potential to resolve many of these manufacturing bottlenecks for highly personalized and time-sensitive nucleic acid therapies by enabling much smaller-scale production of nucleic acid cargo and shortening timelines for platform modification. By manufacturing PFVs separately from their cargo, large batches of PFVs can be manufactured ahead of time, in a process analogous to normal LNP production. PFVs can then be combined at the point-of-care with nucleic acid cargo, which can be developed on much shorter timelines and in appropriate quantities for small-scale administration. 3 Conventional and PFV-based methods of therapeutic delivery vary in the required batch size of the RNA-LNP product, the timing of final-product formulation, and their storage requirements. Acuitas Therapeutics Moreover, manufacturing and shipping PFVs separately from nucleic acid cargo allows for tailored preservation and storage techniques that are less dependent on cold-chain shipping and storage for the delivery vehicle (The nucleic acid cargo may still require cold-chain shipping and storage). Compared to pre-assembled therapies, PFVs can be stored at higher temperatures and shipped in a liquid format while maintaining stability. Preclinical Evidence Sets the Stage for Clinical Development Preclinical testing demonstrates that PFVs can be assembled with nucleic acid cargo within 10–20 minutes at the point-of-care without heat or solvents. With optimized buffer, researchers observed over 90 percent encapsulation efficiency across a variety of payloads, including mRNA, siRNA, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), and mRNA/gRNA mixes at a 1:1 ratio. Due to the reduced interaction time between LNP and mRNA, the PFV process has shown decreased formation of unwanted RNA-lipid adducts compared to conventional mixing methods. 3 Physical and chemical analysis of formulations produced by the conventional and PFV methods show that the particle properties are indistinguishable between both processes. These measurements included particle size and polydispersity index, encapsulation efficiency, RNA content, lipid content, and RNA integrity. Moreover, morphological analysis by cryo-EM imaging showed equivalent particles, and PFV loaded with mRNA demonstrated stability for over 40 weeks in liquid-format storage conditions (2–8 o C). 3 The most compelling stability readout showed unloaded PFV’s unique ability to retain encapsulation efficacy across all time points over a 12 month period when stored in non-frozen, liquid form (4 o C) or cryopreserved (-80 o C), while retaining colloidal stability (unchanging size and a polydispersity index under 0.1) across storage conditions. 3 The capacity for long-term storage suggests the delivery vehicle of a nucleic acid therapy can be stored in bulk at the point-of-care so that the timing of therapeutic administration is primarily contingent upon the availability of nucleic acid cargo. LNP-RNA products manufactured through the standard loading process (Std) and the PFV process demonstrate equivalent hemagglutinin (HA) antigen response across LNP ionizable lipid compositions. Acuitas Therapeutics In a proof-of-concept where the PFV was produced immediately before administration, researchers demonstrated equivalent performance between the two delivery methods across different applications: prophylactic vaccines and systemically administered therapeutics. For an mRNA vaccine encoding an influenza hemagglutinin (HA) antigen, functional antibody response was statistically equivalent between conventional LNP and PFV. For systemically administered therapeutics, comparable serum antibody expression was also achieved following delivery of mRNA encoding a monoclonal antibody. 3 While PFVs have yet to be applied in clinical trials, preclinical evidence to date supports the long-term potential to improve the feasibility of programmable medicine. Drug developers working on vaccine strategies for rapidly evolving pathogens and those working on highly personalized and programmable nucleic acid medicines may benefit from an investment in this novel manufacturing strategy. LNP-RNA products encoding the monoclonal antibody IgG that are manufactured through the standard loading process (Conventional mixing) and the point-of-care PFV process have comparable serum antibody expression response. Acuitas Therapeutics A Convergence of Nucleic Acid Therapeutic Innovation The PFV manufacturing method converges in time with many other advancements that are broadening the accessibility and applications of nucleic acid medicines. Improved understanding of nucleic acid and disease biology is expanding the forms and applications of nucleic acid cargo. 1,4 Change is incremental but hastened by the collaboration of teams who bring together diverse solutions and approaches to better address enduring threats to human health and well-being. T he Elegance of Nucleic Acid Therapy is Compromised by Logistic Complexity Conventional biologics are static; their structure and mechanism are fixed once they are developed. In contrast, nucleic acid therapies are inherently programmable—putting treatments once thought to be impossible within reach. The attractiveness of using RNA or DNA as a therapeutic comes from the nature of a nucleic acid itself, which can encode a plethora of biological outcomes based on the type of nucleic acid and the nucleotide sequence. 1 To elicit a targeted immune response, mRNA encoding an antigen can function as a vaccine, while mRNA encoding antibodies can mimic an adaptive immune response. To intervene at the level of disease-causing molecular mechanisms, siRNA can silence disease-causing genes; mRNA can replace missing proteins; and targeted gene editing can be achieved when a guide RNA is paired with mRNA encoding a gene editor. 1 Small adjustments to a nucleic acid design enable further tailoring of a nucleic acid therapy’s mechanism of action, and can lead to improvements in stability, potency, and safety. This enables amendments at the drug substrate level without changing the overall drug product design. 1 For instance, modifying the coding sequence of an antigenic protein can allow an mRNA vaccine platform to be adapted to the biology of a specific recipient or pathogenic target, without changing the overarching approach or mechanism. Yet, current manufacturing and delivery models for nucleic acid therapies are based on processes that assume large-batch production of a fixed product, and this limits the inherent flexibility of nucleic acid therapeutics, thus reducing their therapeutic application. 2 An alternative process that combines cargo-agnostic pre-formed vesicles (PFVs) with the customizable therapeutic agent at the point-of-care could help nucleic acid therapies enable personalized medicines. 3 How Are Nucleic Acid Therapies Made Today? This type of therapy includes a highly fragile and biologically reactive nucleic acid cargo, which acts as the therapeutic agent, and a delivery vehicle, which encapsulates the cargo to protect it and facilitate entry into target cells. A commonly used and clinically validated delivery vehicle for nucleic acid therapies, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), are constructed from a precise mix of ionizable lipids, structural lipids, and steric lipids—each playing a critical role. These include interacting with, encapsulating, and protecting the nucleic acid payload. Together, the formulation of an LNP determines how well it maintains stability and purity during manufacturing and administration as well as the success of cellular delivery and uptake. 4 For special applications, LNPs can be decorated with ligands which enable cell-specific delivery. Current manufacturing and shipping processes for nucleic acid therapies involve loading the delivery vehicle with the nucleic acid cargo upfront. This requires relatively large batch sizes and complex procedures to maintain the integrity and stability of the product over time. 2 In this loading process, the lipid components of the LNPs are combined and dissolved in an organic solvent (typically ethanol), and rapidly mixed with the nucleic acid cargo suspended in an acidic buffer, assembling themselves into LNPs that completely encapsulate the nucleic acid therapeutic. The ethanol must then be removed and replaced with an isotonic neutral pH buffer to stabilize the loaded LNPs, before the products are prepared for cryopreservation, vialed, frozen, and shipped via cold-chain (typically -20°C to -80°C). 2 While working on the COMIRNATY™ vaccine process with Pfizer and BioNTech, we found that this manufacturing model is sensible when large batches of a nucleic acid therapy are needed to address a pandemic-scale response. 4 However, the resulting products required cold-chain infrastructure and needed to be received and administered by hospital personnel trained in handling cryopreserved products, limiting vaccine access in low-resource settings. The manufacturing model was also wasteful; as the COVID-19 virus mutated, the efficacy of the original vaccine design waned, necessitating a yearly update to the formulation. Re-manufacturing the vaccine with an updated mRNA sequence led to the waste of the previous year’s unused vaccines. In most contexts where a nucleic acid therapy’s modality is most promising, upfront batch-based production is counterproductive, necessitating over-production that increases the cost of a nucleic acid therapy on a per-dose basis. The excessive minimum-batch sizes of current production methods limit the economic feasibility of single, small-batch therapies and of therapeutic iteration. Meanwhile, pre-loading of the delivery vehicle with nucleic acid cargo ties therapeutic modification-to-administration turnaround times to the combined manufacturing, release, and shipping process which can take upwards of six months. 2 Processes that enable smaller-scale production and shorter turnaround times between therapeutic modification and administration are needed to propel rapidly programmable medicines from possibility to clinical reality. Pre-formed Vesicles Could Resolve LNP Manufacturing Bottlenecks Loading PFVs with their nucleic acid cargo at the point-of-care has the potential to resolve many of these manufacturing bottlenecks for highly personalized and time-sensitive nucleic acid therapies by enabling much smaller-scale production of nucleic acid cargo and shortening timelines for platform modification. By manufacturing PFVs separately from their cargo, large batches of PFVs can be manufactured ahead of time, in a process analogous to normal LNP production. PFVs can then be combined at the point-of-care with nucleic acid cargo, which can be developed on much shorter timelines and in appropriate quantities for small-scale administration. 3 Conventional and PFV-based methods of therapeutic delivery vary in the required batch size of the RNA-LNP product, the timing of final-product formulation, and their storage requirements. Acuitas Therapeutics Moreover, manufacturing and shipping PFVs separately from nucleic acid cargo allows for tailored preservation and storage techniques that are less dependent on cold-chain shipping and storage for the delivery vehicle (The nucleic acid cargo may still require cold-chain shipping and storage). Compared to pre-assembled therapies, PFVs can be stored at higher temperatures and shipped in a liquid format while maintaining stability. Preclinical Evidence Sets the Stage for Clinical Development Preclinical testing demonstrates that PFVs can be assembled with nucleic acid cargo within 10–20 minutes at the point-of-care without heat or solvents. With optimized buffer, researchers observed over 90 percent encapsulation efficiency across a variety of payloads, including mRNA, siRNA, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), and mRNA/gRNA mixes at a 1:1 ratio. Due to the reduced interaction time between LNP and mRNA, the PFV process has shown decreased formation of unwanted RNA-lipid adducts compared to conventional mixing methods. 3 Physical and chemical analysis of formulations produced by the conventional and PFV methods show that the particle properties are indistinguishable between both processes. These measurements included particle size and polydispersity index, encapsulation efficiency, RNA content, lipid content, and RNA integrity. Moreover, morphological analysis by cryo-EM imaging showed equivalent particles, and PFV loaded with mRNA demonstrated stability for over 40 weeks in liquid-format storage conditions (2–8 o C). 3 The most compelling stability readout showed unloaded PFV’s unique ability to retain encapsulation efficacy across all time points over a 12 month period when stored in non-frozen, liquid form (4 o C) or cryopreserved (-80 o C), while retaining colloidal stability (unchanging size and a polydispersity index under 0.1) across storage conditions. 3 The capacity for long-term storage suggests the delivery vehicle of a nucleic acid therapy can be stored in bulk at the point-of-care so that the timing of therapeutic administration is primarily contingent upon the availability of nucleic acid cargo. LNP-RNA products manufactured through the standard loading process (Std) and the PFV process demonstrate equivalent hemagglutinin (HA) antigen response across LNP ionizable lipid compositions. Acuitas Therapeutics In a proof-of-concept where the PFV was produced immediately before administration, researchers demonstrated equivalent performance between the two delivery methods across different applications: prophylactic vaccines and systemically administered therapeutics. For an mRNA vaccine encoding an influenza hemagglutinin (HA) antigen, functional antibody response was statistically equivalent between conventional LNP and PFV. For systemically administered therapeutics, comparable serum antibody expression was also achieved following delivery of mRNA encoding a monoclonal antibody. 3 While PFVs have yet to be applied in clinical trials, preclinical evidence to date supports the long-term potential to improve the feasibility of programmable medicine. Drug developers working on vaccine strategies for rapidly evolving pathogens and those working on highly personalized and programmable nucleic acid medicines may benefit from an investment in this novel manufacturing strategy. LNP-RNA products encoding the monoclonal antibody IgG that are manufactured through the standard loading process (Conventional mixing) and the point-of-care PFV process have comparable serum antibody expression response. Acuitas Therapeutics A Convergence of Nucleic Acid Therapeutic Innovation The PFV manufacturing method converges in time with many other advancements that are broadening the accessibility and applications of nucleic acid medicines. Improved understanding of nucleic acid and disease biology is expanding the forms and applications of nucleic acid cargo. 1,4 Change is incremental but hastened by the collaboration of teams who bring together diverse solutions and approaches to better address enduring threats to human health and well-being. Preclinical testing demonstrates that PFVs can be assembled with nucleic acid cargo within 10–20 minutes at the point-of-care without heat or solvents. These measurements included particle size and polydispersity index, encapsulation efficiency, RNA content, lipid content, and RNA integrity. A Convergence of Nucleic Acid Therapeutic Innovation
The PFV manufacturing method converges in time with many other advancements that are broadening the accessibility and applications of nucleic acid medicines. I am Deepika Godugu , and I am currently a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences at St. John’s University. My research focuses on anticancer drug development and evaluation, with expertise in both in vitro cell-based assays and in vivo tumor models. I have a strong background in pharmaceutical sciences, cancer biology, and advanced drug delivery systems, including nanotechnology-based formulations. My technical skills include molecular biology techniques such as Western blotting, flow cytometry, PCR, and functional gene silencing approaches including shRNA transfection and lentiviral transduction. Q | How did you first get interested in science and/or your field of research? My interest in science began during my undergraduate studies in pharmacy, where I was fascinated by how molecular mechanisms could be targeted to treat disease. This curiosity deepened during my PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences, where I worked on developing and evaluating novel drug delivery systems for cancer therapy. Witnessing the limitations of conventional treatments, especially in oncology, motivated me to explore innovative approaches such as nanomedicine, targeted delivery, and molecular interventions. I was particularly drawn to translational research that bridges laboratory discoveries with clinical applications. My postdoctoral work at St. John’s University has allowed me to combine in vitro assays, in vivo tumor models, and molecular biology techniques such as shRNA-mediated gene silencing to better understand therapeutic mechanisms and resistance pathways. This integration of basic science with potential real-world impact continues to inspire my research, with the ultimate goal of improving patient outcomes through more precise and effective therapies. One of my favorite research projects focuses on developing a nanoparticle-based formulation to enhance the delivery and efficacy of an anticancer compound with poor bioavailability. This project is exciting because it combines my expertise in pharmaceutical formulation with molecular biology approaches to evaluate therapeutic mechanisms. Using in vitro cancer cell models and in vivo tumor-bearing mice, we assess not only the drug’s cytotoxicity but also its ability to modulate specific molecular pathways linked to tumor growth and resistance. What I find most rewarding is the translational potential our preclinical results show promising tumor regression and reduced systemic toxicity, bringing the formulation a step closer to potential clinical application. The project also incorporates advanced techniques like shRNA-mediated gene silencing to dissect the drug’s mechanism of action, which adds a deeper mechanistic layer to our findings. Seeing the intersection of formulation science, molecular targeting, and therapeutic efficacy makes this work both challenging and inspiring. Q | What has been the most exciting part of your scientific career/journey so far? The most exciting part of my scientific journey so far has been seeing a research concept evolve from an initial idea to promising preclinical results with real translational potential. During my PhD and postdoctoral work, I have had the opportunity to design novel drug formulations, test them in both cell-based and animal models, and uncover their molecular mechanisms of action. One highlight was developing a nanoparticle-based anticancer formulation that significantly improved therapeutic efficacy and reduced toxicity in vivo. Watching data emerge that could eventually inform better treatment strategies was both professionally fulfilling and personally motivating. Moments like these when rigorous experimentation leads to discoveries that could meaningfully impact patient care reinforce why I chose a career in translational cancer research. I am Deepika Godugu , and I am currently a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences at St. John’s University. My research focuses on anticancer drug development and evaluation, with expertise in both in vitro cell-based assays and in vivo tumor models. I have a strong background in pharmaceutical sciences, cancer biology, and advanced drug delivery systems, including nanotechnology-based formulations. My technical skills include molecular biology techniques such as Western blotting, flow cytometry, PCR, and functional gene silencing approaches including shRNA transfection and lentiviral transduction. Q | How did you first get interested in science and/or your field of research? My interest in science began during my undergraduate studies in pharmacy, where I was fascinated by how molecular mechanisms could be targeted to treat disease. This curiosity deepened during my PhD in Pharmaceutical Sciences, where I worked on developing and evaluating novel drug delivery systems for cancer therapy. Witnessing the limitations of conventional treatments, especially in oncology, motivated me to explore innovative approaches such as nanomedicine, targeted delivery, and molecular interventions. I was particularly drawn to translational research that bridges laboratory discoveries with clinical applications. My postdoctoral work at St. John’s University has allowed me to combine in vitro assays, in vivo tumor models, and molecular biology techniques such as shRNA-mediated gene silencing to better understand therapeutic mechanisms and resistance pathways. This integration of basic science with potential real-world impact continues to inspire my research, with the ultimate goal of improving patient outcomes through more precise and effective therapies. One of my favorite research projects focuses on developing a nanoparticle-based formulation to enhance the delivery and efficacy of an anticancer compound with poor bioavailability. This project is exciting because it combines my expertise in pharmaceutical formulation with molecular biology approaches to evaluate therapeutic mechanisms. Using in vitro cancer cell models and in vivo tumor-bearing mice, we assess not only the drug’s cytotoxicity but also its ability to modulate specific molecular pathways linked to tumor growth and resistance. What I find most rewarding is the translational potential our preclinical results show promising tumor regression and reduced systemic toxicity, bringing the formulation a step closer to potential clinical application. The project also incorporates advanced techniques like shRNA-mediated gene silencing to dissect the drug’s mechanism of action, which adds a deeper mechanistic layer to our findings. Seeing the intersection of formulation science, molecular targeting, and therapeutic efficacy makes this work both challenging and inspiring.
